questions.title: What a data dictionary is
questions.text: What is a **data dictionary**?

options.content: A list of the words used in a program
A document that describes the structure of a database: every field with its type, size, format, key and validation
A backup copy of all the records in a database
A table that stores the users' passwords

scheme.mark_scheme: B

questions.title: Why a data dictionary is used
questions.text: Select **three** reasons why a data dictionary is used.

options.content: The same field has the same name and data type in every table
It makes the computer's processor faster
Programmers can build the tables and write SQL correctly
It replaces the need for a primary key
Validation rules are recorded, so invalid data is rejected
It stores the records of the database

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C and E. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: What is recorded
questions.text: Select **two** items that are recorded in a data dictionary for each field.

options.content: Data type
The name of the user who last edited the record
Validation rule
The colour of the input form

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Metadata
questions.text: A data dictionary stores the actual records of the database, such as each pupil's name and marks.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: It stores metadata — descriptions of the fields — not the data itself.

questions.title: Who uses a data dictionary
questions.text: Match each person to how they use the data dictionary.

right.text: Creates the tables and writes queries and forms
Chooses test data from the validation rules
Maintains and changes the database later

scheme.mark_scheme: Database designer – Plans the tables and fields; Programmer – Creates the tables and writes queries and forms; Tester – Chooses test data from the validation rules; Database administrator – Maintains and changes the database later.

questions.title: Validation checks
questions.text: Match each validation rule to the type of check.

left.text: Surname must not be left empty
Pupil ID must be S followed by 4 digits

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–Range, L2–Presence, L3–Format, L4–Lookup. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Choose data types
questions.text: Complete the data dictionary with the most suitable data type for each field. Use: **VARCHAR**, **INTEGER**, **DECIMAL**, **DATE**, **BOOLEAN**.

scheme.mark_scheme: MemberID VARCHAR (1); JoinDate DATE (1); MonthlyFee DECIMAL (1); Visits INTEGER (1); IsActive BOOLEAN (1)

questions.title: Write validation rules
questions.text: Complete the data dictionary with a suitable **validation rule** for each field.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Age (1): range check, e.g. 6–100 / > 0
Email (1): format check — contains @ and a dot / presence / uniqueness
Password (1): length check, e.g. 8–16 characters / presence
Size (1): lookup check — S, M, L, XL
scheme.model_answer: Age: range check 6–100. Email: format check — must contain @. Password: length check 8–16 characters. Size: lookup check — S, M, L or XL.
scheme.ai_instructions: Each rule must be sensible for that field; name of the check is not required if the rule is clear.

questions.title: Data type for a phone number
questions.text: A designer gives the field `Phone` the data type INTEGER. Explain why this is not suitable and state a better data type.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A phone number may start with + or 0 / contain spaces; no calculations are done; may be too long for an integer (1)
- VARCHAR / text (1)
scheme.model_answer: A phone number such as +77011234567 contains a + sign and is never used in calculations, so it should be stored as VARCHAR.

questions.title: Foreign key type
questions.text: In a data dictionary, `StudentID` is VARCHAR(5) in the `Students` table. Explain why `StudentID` in the `Loans` table must also be VARCHAR(5).

scheme.mark_scheme:
- It is a foreign key that refers to the primary key in Students (1)
- the values must match exactly for the tables to be linked / joined / referential integrity (1)

points.criterion: Foreign key referring to the PK

scheme.model_answer: StudentID in Loans is a foreign key referring to the primary key of Students, so its values must be of the same type and size to match and link the two tables.

questions.title: Validation limits
questions.text: A range check allows dates of birth between 2005 and 2012. Explain why a pupil's date of birth could still be stored incorrectly.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Validation only checks that data is sensible / within the rules (1)
- a wrong date inside the range (e.g. a typing mistake) would still be accepted; verification is needed (1)
scheme.model_answer: Validation only checks that the date is in the allowed range; if 15/04/2009 is typed instead of 14/04/2009, it is still accepted even though it is wrong.

questions.title: Format rule
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

The rule "BookID must be the letter B followed by five digits" is a [[1]] check. The rule "Quantity must not be negative" is a [[2]] check.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) format / picture (2) range

questions.title: Create an entry
questions.text: Complete the data dictionary entry for the field `Price` in a `Products` table.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Data type: DECIMAL / REAL / CURRENCY (1)
Key: none (1)
Validation: range check > 0 / presence (1)
Example: e.g. 450.00 (1)
scheme.model_answer: Price | DECIMAL | — | Range check: greater than 0 | 450.00

questions.title: A library data dictionary
questions.text:
```text
Books ( BookID, Title, Author, YearPublished, Available )
```

parts.title: Data types
parts.text: Complete the data type for each field.

scheme.mark_scheme: Title VARCHAR (1); YearPublished INTEGER (1); Available BOOLEAN (1)

parts.title: Validation
parts.text: State a suitable validation rule for `BookID` and for `YearPublished`.

scheme.mark_scheme:
BookID (1): presence / uniqueness / format, e.g. B + 5 digits
YearPublished (1): range, e.g. 1450 to the current year
scheme.model_answer: BookID: format check — B followed by 5 digits. YearPublished: range check 1450 to 2026.

parts.title: Primary key

scheme.mark_scheme: BookID (1)

questions.title: Create a data dictionary
questions.text:
A cinema stores tickets in the table:

```text
Tickets ( TicketID, FilmID, SeatNumber, ShowDate, Price, IsChild )
```

Create a data dictionary for this table. For each field give the data type, key (if any) and a validation rule.

scheme.mark_scheme:
One mark per field correctly described (data type + sensible key / validation) (max 6):
- TicketID: INTEGER / VARCHAR, PK, unique / presence
- FilmID: same type as Films PK, FK, must exist in Films
- SeatNumber: VARCHAR (e.g. A12), format letter + digits
- ShowDate: DATE, not in the past / presence
- Price: DECIMAL, range > 0
- IsChild: BOOLEAN, true / false
scheme.model_answer:
TicketID | INTEGER | PK | unique, presence
FilmID | VARCHAR(6) | FK → Films | must exist in Films
SeatNumber | VARCHAR(3) | — | format: letter + 1–2 digits (A12)
ShowDate | DATE | — | presence; not before today
Price | DECIMAL | — | range > 0
IsChild | BOOLEAN | — | True / False

questions.title: Data dictionaries
questions.text: A developer is designing a database for a sports club and writes a data dictionary.

parts.title: Purpose
parts.text: Explain the purpose of a data dictionary.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): describes every field / metadata; consistent names, types, sizes; programmers build the database correctly; validation rules → integrity; maintenance / documentation
scheme.model_answer: It describes each field's name, type, size and validation so the database is built consistently, and it helps developers maintain the database later.

parts.title: Items recorded
parts.text: State **two** items, other than the field name, recorded for each field.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): data type; size / length; format; key; validation rule; required / null; description; example

parts.title: Who uses it
parts.text: Describe how a **programmer** would use the data dictionary.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): to create the tables with the correct field names / types / sizes; to set keys; to write validation / input forms; to write queries / code using the exact field names
scheme.model_answer: The programmer uses it to create each table with the exact field names, data types and keys, and to add the validation rules to the input forms.

parts.title: Integrity
parts.text: Explain how the validation rules in a data dictionary improve data integrity.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Rules are applied when data is entered, so unreasonable / invalid data is rejected (1)
- the stored data is more accurate / consistent (1)
scheme.model_answer: The rules are built into the database, so data that breaks them, such as an age of 250, is rejected at entry, which keeps the stored data accurate and consistent.

summary: What a data dictionary is and why it is used, what it records about each field (name, data type, size, format, key, validation, description, example), and how to create a data dictionary for the tables of a database.

blocks.content: A **document or table that describes the structure of a database** — "data about the data" (**metadata**). For every **table** it lists every **field** with its **name, data type, size, format, key, validation rules, description** and an **example**.
**Data that describes other data.** The value `14/03/2009` is data; the facts "this field is called `DateOfBirth`, it is a Date in the format DD/MM/YYYY and it must be filled in" are metadata.

blocks.title: What a data dictionary records for each field
rows: The exact name used in the database (no spaces)
Text / VARCHAR, Integer, Real / Decimal, Date, Boolean
Maximum number of characters or digits
How the data is displayed or entered
Primary key (PK), foreign key (FK) or none
The rule the data must satisfy
Whether the field must have a value

blocks.content: The data dictionary also records information about each **table**: its name, what it stores, its primary key and how it is linked to other tables (the relationships from the ERD).

blocks.text: Data types in a data dictionary

blocks.title: Common data types
rows: Letters, digits and symbols, up to *n* characters

blocks.content: A phone number such as `+7 701 234 56 78` is stored as **Text**, not as a number: it can start with `+` or `0`, contains spaces, and nobody does arithmetic with it.

items.title: Good field names
items.content:
- **No spaces** — `DateOfBirth` or `date_of_birth`, not `Date of birth`.
- **Meaningful** — `Surname`, not `Field3` or `S`.
- **One style** for the whole database (e.g. CamelCase everywhere).
- **The same name** for the same data in every table — `StudentID` in `Students` and in `Loans`.

items.title: Why it matters
items.content:
- Programmers write field names in SQL and code; spaces and different spellings cause errors.
- Matching names make the links between tables (primary key → foreign key) easy to see.
- The data dictionary is the place where these names are **agreed and written down**.

theory.title: The purpose of a data dictionary

items.title: Why a data dictionary is used
items.content:
- Gives **one clear, agreed definition** of every field, so everyone uses the same names and types.
- Helps **programmers build** the database and write code / SQL correctly.
- Ensures **consistency** — the same field (e.g. `StudentID`) has the same type and size in every table, so keys match.
- Records **validation rules**, which improves **data integrity** (fewer invalid entries).
- Helps **maintenance** — new developers understand the database quickly; changes are documented.
- Forms part of the **technical documentation** of the system.

items.title: Who uses it
items.content:
- **Database designers** and **analysts** — to plan the tables.
- **Programmers** — to create the tables and write queries and forms.
- **Testers** — to choose test data from the validation rules.
- **Database administrators** — to maintain and change the database later.

blocks.title: What goes wrong without a data dictionary
blocks.content:
A school's database was built by two programmers who did not agree on the fields:
- `StudentID` is **Text** in one table and **Integer** in another — the tables cannot be joined, so loan reports show no names.
- One form saves dates as `05/11/2026`, another as `2026-11-05` — searches by date miss half the records.
- Nobody wrote down that `Mark` must be 0–100 — a mark of `750` was typed and the class average became wrong.
- A new programmer has to read all the code to guess what `Fld7` means.

A data dictionary written at the design stage prevents every one of these problems.

theory.title: Exam practice: what a data dictionary is

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Define the term data dictionary. [1]**
A document / table that describes the structure of a database — the fields of every table with their data types, sizes, formats, keys and validation (data about the data / metadata) (1).

**Q: State three items stored in a data dictionary for each field. [3]**
Any three: field name, data type, field size, format, key (PK / FK), validation rule, description, example value.

**Q: Explain two reasons why a data dictionary is used. [4]**
It gives **consistent definitions**, so the same field has the same name and type in every table (1) and keys between tables match / the tables can be linked (1). It records **validation rules** (1), so invalid data is rejected and data integrity improves (1). *(Also: helps programmers build the database; helps maintenance / new developers.)*

**Q: Explain why a phone number is stored as text. [2]**
It may begin with `0` or `+` and contain spaces, which a number field would lose / not allow (1); no calculations are done with it (1).

- Writing that a data dictionary **stores the data** — it stores **metadata**, the description of the data.
- Listing only "name and type" — exam answers expect **size, format, key, validation** too.
- Vague reasons like "it organises the database" — say **who** it helps and **what problem** it prevents.

blocks.title: Validation checks
rows: The data is the **correct data type**
Pupil ID `S` followed by 4 digits, e.g. S0421
The value is in a **list of allowed values**
Grade is 11 or 12; Gender is M or F
No two records have the same value

blocks.content: **Validation** checks that data is **sensible / reasonable** (it follows the rules). It cannot check that the data is **correct** — "15/04/2009" passes a date check even if the pupil was born on 14/04/2009.

blocks.title: How to create a data dictionary
items: List the **tables** of the database (from the ERD).
For each table, list every **field** with a clear name (no spaces).
Choose the most suitable **data type** and **size** for each field.
Mark the **primary key** and any **foreign keys** (a foreign key must have the **same type and size** as the primary key it refers to).
Add a **validation rule**, a **format** where needed, a short **description** and an **example**.

blocks.title: Data dictionary for a school library — table `Students`
blocks.content:
| Field name | Data type | Size | Key | Validation | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| StudentID | VARCHAR | 5 | PK | Presence; format `S` + 4 digits; unique | Unique student number | S0421 |
| FirstName | VARCHAR | 30 | | Presence | Student's first name | Aruzhan |
| Surname | VARCHAR | 30 | | Presence | Student's family name | Bekova |
| Grade | INTEGER | 2 | | Lookup: 11 or 12 | School grade | 11 |
| DateOfBirth | DATE | — | | Range 01/01/2005 – 31/12/2012 | Date of birth, DD/MM/YYYY | 14/03/2009 |
| Phone | VARCHAR | 12 | | Length 12; format `+7` + 10 digits | Contact phone | +77011234567 |

blocks.title: Data dictionary — table `Loans`
blocks.content:
| Field name | Data type | Size | Key | Validation | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| LoanID | INTEGER | — | PK | Unique; auto-increment | Loan number | 1057 |
| StudentID | VARCHAR | 5 | FK → Students | Must exist in Students | Who borrowed the book | S0421 |
| BookID | VARCHAR | 6 | FK → Books | Must exist in Books | Which book | B00312 |
| LoanDate | DATE | — | | Presence; not in the future | Date borrowed | 02/10/2026 |
| ReturnDate | DATE | — | | Must be on or after LoanDate (may be empty) | Date returned | 16/10/2026 |
| Returned | BOOLEAN | — | | True / False | Has the book been returned? | False |

CREATE TABLE Students (
    StudentID   VARCHAR(5)  PRIMARY KEY,
    FirstName   VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    Surname     VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    Grade       INTEGER     CHECK (Grade IN (11, 12)),
    DateOfBirth DATE,
    Phone       VARCHAR(12)
);
blocks.caption: The data dictionary turned into SQL

blocks.content:
- Numbers you **calculate with** → INTEGER or REAL/DECIMAL (price → DECIMAL).
- **Codes and numbers you do not calculate with** (phone, ID, postcode) → VARCHAR / TEXT.
- **Yes/No** values → BOOLEAN.
- Dates → DATE (so they can be sorted and compared correctly).

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Explain the purpose of a data dictionary. [2]**
It **describes every field** of the database — name, data type, size, validation (1) — so that programmers **build the database consistently and correctly** and it is easier to **maintain** later (1).

**Q: Complete the data dictionary entry for the field `Price`. [3]**
Data type: **Decimal / Real** (1); validation: **range check > 0** (1); example: **450.00** (1).

**Q: State why a foreign key must have the same data type and size as the primary key it refers to. [1]**
So that the values **match** and the tables can be **linked** (joined) correctly.

- Using INTEGER for phone numbers or IDs with letters or leading zeros.
- Writing validation that does not match the data (a range check on a name).
- Giving a description that just repeats the field name ("Surname — the surname").
- Forgetting to mark **primary** and **foreign** keys.
- Confusing a data dictionary with a **user guide** — it is **technical** documentation.
